# awsm-renderer-scene-loader

Loads an `awsm-renderer-scene` runtime bundle (`scene.toml` + `assets/`) into the
renderer. The parallel to `awsm-renderer-gltf`'s `populate_gltf`: that loads
*foreign* glTF, this loads *our* format. They share the same renderer core — glb
meshes in a bundle go through `populate_gltf`'s machinery, primitives regenerate
via `awsm-renderer-meshgen`, and our materials / clips bind on top.

## What's here

- `populate_awsm_scene(renderer, scene, assets, on_phase)`— the entry point. Loads the node hierarchy (transforms), primitive + glb + skinned meshes, lights (with shadow params), cameras, textures, custom-WGSL materials, and animation clips + the NLA mixer. Returns a- `LoadedScene`of the inserted handles for later teardown.
- Submodules: `material`,`texture`,`dynamic`(custom-WGSL),`light`,`camera`,`animation`.

`assets` is an in-memory map of bundle-relative paths → bytes, so loading never
touches disk. `on_phase` reports each `LoadPhase` boundary (through pipeline
compile) for live progress; pass `|_| {}` to ignore it.

## Batched, phased load

The work runs as one phased pass, efficient for the player's typical "load a bundle then render" case:

- **Build materials**— lower every node's authored material and insert once, so meshes (including glb meshes via- `GltfMaterialSource::Single`) reference a ready key instead of letting the glTF loader mint a throwaway default.
- **Upload textures**— one batched- `finalize_gpu_textures`for the whole scene.
- **Upload meshes**— transforms + geometry (+ skins) + lights. The scene's animation clips + NLA mixer are then lowered against the per-node keys built in the prior phases (this step reports no separate- `LoadPhase`).
- **Compile pipelines**— one drive-to-ready for all materials + shadows, so the first frame draws everything rather than trickling pipelines across frames.

The headline consumer is the **round-trip test**: in the MCP-controlled browser
session, `export_player_bundle` → `populate_awsm_scene` → screenshot, compared
against the source render. The loader only LOADS clips; the consumer drives the
clock (a player's `update_animations`, or the editor round-trip's playhead pin).

## Companion crates

- `awsm-renderer-scene`— the runtime schema this loads.
- `awsm-renderer`/- `awsm-renderer-gltf`— the renderer core and the shared glTF upload path it reuses.

# ferridriver_bdd_macros - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ferridriver-bdd-macros/0.5.0/ferridriver_bdd_macros/

## Expand description

Proc macros for the ferridriver BDD/Cucumber framework.

Provides step definition macros that register async handler functions
via `inventory` for automatic collection at runtime.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use ferridriver_bdd::prelude::*;
#[given("I navigate to {string}")]
async fn navigate(world: &mut BrowserWorld, url: String) {
    world.page().goto(&url, None).await.map_err(|e| step_err!("{e}"))?;
}
#[when("I click {string}")]
async fn click(world: &mut BrowserWorld, selector: String) {
    world.page().locator(&selector, None).click(None).await.map_err(|e| step_err!("{e}"))?;
}
#[then("the page title should be {string}")]
async fn check_title(world: &mut BrowserWorld, expected: String) {
    let title = world.page().title().await.map_err(|e| step_err!("{e}"))?;
    assert_eq!(title, expected);
}
```
## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [after](https://docs.rs/attr.after.html)
- Register an After hook.
- [before](https://docs.rs/attr.before.html)
- Register a Before hook.
- [given](https://docs.rs/attr.given.html)
- Register a Given step definition.
- [param_](https://docs.rs/attr.param_type.html)- type
- Register a custom parameter type for Cucumber expressions.
- [step](https://docs.rs/attr.step.html)
- Register a keyword-agnostic step definition (matches Given/When/Then).
- [then](https://docs.rs/attr.then.html)
- Register a Then step definition.
- [when](https://docs.rs/attr.when.html)
- Register a When step definition.

# ferridriver_test_macros - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ferridriver-test-macros/0.5.0/ferridriver_test_macros/

## Expand description

Proc macros for the ferridriver test framework.

Provides `#[ferritest]` to register async browser test functions. The
annotated function takes a single `TestContext`; built-in fixtures
(`page`, `browser`, `context`, …) resolve lazily through it.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use ferridriver_test::prelude::*;
#[ferritest]
async fn basic_navigation(ctx: TestContext) {
    let page = ctx.page().await?;
    page.goto("https://example.com", None).await?;
    expect(&page).to_have_title("Example").await?;
}
#[ferritest(retries = 2, timeout = "30s", tag = "smoke")]
async fn flaky_test(ctx: TestContext) {
    let page = ctx.page().await?;
    let context = ctx.browser_context().await?;
    // ...
}
```
## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [after_](https://docs.rs/attr.after_all.html)- all
- Runs once after all tests in the containing module (suite).
- [after_](https://docs.rs/attr.after_each.html)- each
- Runs after each test in the containing module (suite), even on failure.
- [before_](https://docs.rs/attr.before_all.html)- all
- Runs once before all tests in the containing module (suite).
- [before_](https://docs.rs/attr.before_each.html)- each
- Runs before each test in the containing module (suite).
- [ferritest](https://docs.rs/attr.ferritest.html)
- `#[ferritest]`attribute macro.
- [ferritest_](https://docs.rs/attr.ferritest_each.html)- each
- `#[ferritest_each(data = [("a", 1), ("b", 2)])]`— parameterized test macro.
- [ferritest_](https://docs.rs/attr.ferritest_suite.html)- suite
- `#[ferritest_suite(mode = "serial")]`— set the execution mode of every- `#[ferritest]`in the annotated module. A serial suite is dispatched as one batch to a single worker, runs in source order, and skips the rest on first failure. The default (no attribute) is parallel.
- [fixture](https://docs.rs/attr.fixture.html)
- `#[fixture]`— register a custom, dependency-injected, scoped fixture.

# token_calibrator - Rust

- `pub use estimator::`- [TokenEstimator](https://docs.rs/estimator/struct.TokenEstimator.html);
- `pub use estimator::`- [TokenEstimatorOptions](https://docs.rs/estimator/struct.TokenEstimatorOptions.html);
- `pub use builtin_rates::`- [BUILTIN_TOKEN_RATES](https://docs.rs/builtin_rates/static.BUILTIN_TOKEN_RATES.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [buckets](https://docs.rs/buckets/index.html)
- Bucketing + pure estimation — the model-blind feature layer.
- [builtin_](https://docs.rs/builtin_rates/index.html)- rates
- Built-in per-model token rates (shipped baseline).
- [calibration](https://docs.rs/calibration/index.html)
- Calibration — the pure ridge-regression math that turns observed
(text, realTokens) rounds into per-bucket rates. Model-blind and stateless;
the stateful writer/reader wrappers live in `calibrator`/`estimator`.
- [calibrator](https://docs.rs/calibrator/index.html)
- TokenCalibrator (writer) — the stateful producer side. Wraps ONE model’s
data-only accumulator: feed it real usage via `observe`, read back solved`rates()`or the raw`to_matrix()`for persistence.
- [estimator](https://docs.rs/estimator/index.html)
- TokenEstimator (reader) — the stateful consumer side (renderer / CLI display).
Built from a `{model: matrix}`map; derives + caches each model’s rates up front. Pure math is in`calibration`; this is per-model lookup plus the shipped-baseline fallback.

---

# base64 0.22.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/base64/0.22.1

Made with CLion. Thanks to JetBrains for supporting open source!

It's base64. What more could anyone want?

This library's goals are to be *correct* and *fast*. It's thoroughly tested and widely used. It exposes functionality at
multiple levels of abstraction so you can choose the level of convenience vs performance that you want,
e.g. `decode_engine_slice` decodes into an existing `&mut [u8]` and is pretty fast (2.6GiB/s for a 3 KiB input),
whereas `decode_engine` allocates a new `Vec<u8>` and returns it, which might be more convenient in some cases, but is
slower (although still fast enough for almost any purpose) at 2.1 GiB/s.

See the [docs](https://docs.rs/base64) for all the details.

## FAQ

### I need to decode base64 with whitespace/null bytes/other random things interspersed in it. What should I do?

Remove non-base64 characters from your input before decoding.

If you have a `Vec` of base64, [retain](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/vec/struct.Vec.html#method.retain) can be used to
strip out whatever you need removed.

If you have a `Read` (e.g. reading a file or network socket), there are various approaches.

- Use [iter_read](https://crates.io/crates/iter-read)together with`Read`'s`bytes()`to filter out unwanted bytes.
- Implement `Read`with a`read()`impl that delegates to your actual`Read`, and then drops any bytes you don't want.

### I need to line-wrap base64, e.g. for MIME/PEM.

[line-wrap](https://crates.io/crates/line-wrap) does just that.

### I want canonical base64 encoding/decoding.

First, don't do this. You should no more expect Base64 to be canonical than you should expect compression algorithms to
produce canonical output across all usage in the wild (hint: they don't).
However, [people are drawn to their own destruction like moths to a flame](https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/361), so here we
are.

There are two opportunities for non-canonical encoding (and thus, detection of the same during decoding): the final bits
of the last encoded token in two or three token suffixes, and the `=` token used to inflate the suffix to a full four
tokens.

The trailing bits issue is unavoidable: with 6 bits available in each encoded token, 1 input byte takes 2 tokens, with the second one having some bits unused. Same for two input bytes: 16 bits, but 3 tokens have 18 bits. Unless we decide to stop shipping whole bytes around, we're stuck with those extra bits that a sneaky or buggy encoder might set to 1 instead of 0.

The `=` pad bytes, on the other hand, are entirely a self-own by the Base64 standard. They do not affect decoding other
than to provide an opportunity to say "that padding is incorrect". Exabytes of storage and transfer have no doubt been
wasted on pointless `=` bytes. Somehow we all seem to be quite comfortable with, say, hex-encoded data just stopping
when it's done rather than requiring a confirmation that the author of the encoder could count to four. Anyway, there
are two ways to make pad bytes predictable: require canonical padding to the next multiple of four bytes as per the RFC,
or, if you control all producers and consumers, save a few bytes by requiring no padding (especially applicable to the
url-safe alphabet).

All `Engine` implementations must at a minimum support treating non-canonical padding of both types as an error, and
optionally may allow other behaviors.

## Rust version compatibility

The minimum supported Rust version is 1.48.0.

# Contributing

Contributions are very welcome. However, because this library is used widely, and in security-sensitive contexts, all PRs will be carefully scrutinized. Beyond that, this sort of low level library simply needs to be 100% correct. Nobody wants to chase bugs in encoding of any sort.

All this means that it takes me a fair amount of time to review each PR, so it might take quite a while to carve out the free time to give each PR the attention it deserves. I will get to everyone eventually!

## Developing

Benchmarks are in `benches/`.

```
## no_std

This crate supports no_std. By default the crate targets std via the `std` feature. You can deactivate
the `default-features` to target `core` instead. In that case you lose out on all the functionality revolving
around `std::io`, `std::error::Error`, and heap allocations. There is an additional `alloc` feature that you can activate
to bring back the support for heap allocations.

## Profiling

On Linux, you can use [perf](https://perf.wiki.kernel.org/index.php/Main_Page) for profiling. Then compile the
benchmarks with `cargo bench --no-run`.

Run the benchmark binary with `perf` (shown here filtering to one particular benchmark, which will make the results
easier to read). `perf` is only available to the root user on most systems as it fiddles with event counters in your
CPU, so use `sudo`. We need to run the actual benchmark binary, hence the path into `target`. You can see the actual
full path with `cargo bench -v`; it will print out the commands it runs. If you use the exact path
that `bench` outputs, make sure you get the one that's for the benchmarks, not the tests. You may also want
to `cargo clean` so you have only one `benchmarks-` binary (they tend to accumulate).

# base64 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/base64/0.22.1/target-redirect/base64/

## Expand description

Correct, fast, and configurable [base64](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/Base64) decoding and encoding. Base64
transports binary data efficiently in contexts where only plain text is
allowed.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Use an [ Engine](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html) to decode or encode base64, configured with the base64
alphabet and padding behavior best suited to your application.

[§](https://docs.rs#engine-setup)Engine setup

There is more than one way to encode a stream of bytes as “base64”.
Different applications use different encoding
[alphabets](https://docs.rs/alphabet/struct.Alphabet.html) and
[padding behaviors](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/struct.GeneralPurposeConfig.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#encoding-alphabet)Encoding alphabet

Almost all base64 [alphabets](https://docs.rs/alphabet/struct.Alphabet.html) use `A-Z`, `a-z`, and
`0-9`, which gives nearly 64 characters (26 + 26 + 10 = 62), but they differ
in their choice of their final 2.

Most applications use the [standard](https://docs.rs/alphabet/constant.STANDARD.html) alphabet specified
in [RFC 4648](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4648#section-4).  If that’s all you need, you can get started
quickly by using the pre-configured
[ STANDARD](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/constant.STANDARD.html) engine, which is also available
in the

[module as shown here, if you prefer a minimal](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)

`prelude``use`
footprint.```
use base64::prelude::*;
assert_eq!(BASE64_STANDARD.decode(b"+uwgVQA=")?, b"\xFA\xEC\x20\x55\0");
assert_eq!(BASE64_STANDARD.encode(b"\xFF\xEC\x20\x55\0"), "/+wgVQA=");
```
Other common alphabets are available in the [ alphabet](https://docs.rs/alphabet/index.html) module.

[§](https://docs.rs#url-safe-alphabet)URL-safe alphabet

The standard alphabet uses `+` and `/` as its two non-alphanumeric tokens,
which cannot be safely used in URL’s without encoding them as `%2B` and
`%2F`.

To avoid that, some applications use a [“URL-safe” alphabet](https://docs.rs/alphabet/constant.URL_SAFE.html),
which uses `-` and `_` instead. To use that alternative alphabet, use the
[ URL_SAFE](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/constant.URL_SAFE.html) engine. This example doesn’t
use

[to show what a more explicit](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)

`prelude``use` would look like.```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::URL_SAFE, Engine as _};
assert_eq!(URL_SAFE.decode(b"-uwgVQA=")?, b"\xFA\xEC\x20\x55\0");
assert_eq!(URL_SAFE.encode(b"\xFF\xEC\x20\x55\0"), "_-wgVQA=");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#padding-characters)Padding characters

Each base64 character represents 6 bits (2⁶ = 64) of the original binary data, and every 3 bytes of input binary data will encode to 4 base64 characters (8 bits × 3 = 6 bits × 4 = 24 bits).

When the input is not an even multiple of 3 bytes in length, [canonical](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4648#section-3.5)
base64 encoders insert padding characters at the end, so that the output
length is always a multiple of 4:

```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::STANDARD, Engine as _};
assert_eq!(STANDARD.encode(b""),    "");
assert_eq!(STANDARD.encode(b"f"),   "Zg==");
assert_eq!(STANDARD.encode(b"fo"),  "Zm8=");
assert_eq!(STANDARD.encode(b"foo"), "Zm9v");
```
Canonical encoding ensures that base64 encodings will be exactly the same,
byte-for-byte, regardless of input length. But the `=` padding characters
aren’t necessary for decoding, and they may be omitted by using a
[ NO_PAD](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/constant.NO_PAD.html) configuration:

```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::STANDARD_NO_PAD, Engine as _};
assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.encode(b""),    "");
assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.encode(b"f"),   "Zg");
assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.encode(b"fo"),  "Zm8");
assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.encode(b"foo"), "Zm9v");
```
The pre-configured `NO_PAD` engines will reject inputs containing padding
`=` characters. To encode without padding and still accept padding while
decoding, create an [engine](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/struct.GeneralPurpose.html) with
that [padding mode](https://docs.rs/engine/enum.DecodePaddingMode.html).

`assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.decode(b"Zm8="), Err(base64::DecodeError::InvalidPadding));`[§](https://docs.rs#further-customization)Further customization

Decoding and encoding behavior can be customized by creating an
[engine](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/struct.GeneralPurpose.html) with an [alphabet](https://docs.rs/alphabet/struct.Alphabet.html) and
[padding configuration](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/struct.GeneralPurposeConfig.html):

```
use base64::{engine, alphabet, Engine as _};
// bizarro-world base64: +/ as the first symbols instead of the last
let alphabet =
    alphabet::Alphabet::new("+/ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789")
    .unwrap();
// a very weird config that encodes with padding but requires no padding when decoding...?
let crazy_config = engine::GeneralPurposeConfig::new()
    .with_decode_allow_trailing_bits(true)
    .with_encode_padding(true)
    .with_decode_padding_mode(engine::DecodePaddingMode::RequireNone);
let crazy_engine = engine::GeneralPurpose::new(&alphabet, crazy_config);
let encoded = crazy_engine.encode(b"abc 123");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#memory-allocation)Memory allocation

The [decode](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html#method.decode) and [encode](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html#method.encode) engine methods
allocate memory for their results – `decode` returns a `Vec<u8>` and
`encode` returns a `String`. To instead decode or encode into a buffer that
you allocated, use one of the alternative methods:

[§](https://docs.rs#decoding)Decoding

| Method | Output | Allocates memory |
|---|---|---|
| `Engine::decode` | returns a new `Vec<u8>` | always |
| `Engine::decode_vec` | appends to provided `Vec<u8>` | if `Vec`lacks capacity |
| `Engine::decode_slice` | writes to provided `&[u8]` | never |

[§](https://docs.rs#encoding)Encoding

| Method | Output | Allocates memory |
|---|---|---|
| `Engine::encode` | returns a new `String` | always |
| `Engine::encode_string` | appends to provided `String` | if `String`lacks capacity |
| `Engine::encode_slice` | writes to provided `&[u8]` | never |

[§](https://docs.rs#input-and-output)Input and output

The `base64` crate can [decode](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html#method.decode) and
[encode](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html#method.encode) values in memory, or
[ DecoderReader](https://docs.rs/read/struct.DecoderReader.html) and

[provide streaming decoding and encoding for any](https://docs.rs/write/struct.EncoderWriter.html)

`EncoderWriter`[readable](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Read.html)or

[writable](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Write.html)byte stream.

[§](https://docs.rs#decoding-1)Decoding

```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::STANDARD, read::DecoderReader};
let mut input = io::stdin();
let mut decoder = DecoderReader::new(&mut input, &STANDARD);
io::copy(&mut decoder, &mut io::stdout())?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#encoding-1)Encoding

```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::STANDARD, write::EncoderWriter};
let mut output = io::stdout();
let mut encoder = EncoderWriter::new(&mut output, &STANDARD);
io::copy(&mut io::stdin(), &mut encoder)?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#display)Display

If you only need a base64 representation for implementing the
[ Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html) trait, use

[:](https://docs.rs/display/struct.Base64Display.html)

`Base64Display````
use base64::{display::Base64Display, engine::general_purpose::STANDARD};
let value = Base64Display::new(b"\0\x01\x02\x03", &STANDARD);
assert_eq!("base64: AAECAw==", format!("base64: {}", value));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

If length calculations result in overflowing `usize`, a panic will result.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use engine::`- [Engine](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [alphabet](https://docs.rs/alphabet/index.html)
- Provides [Alphabet](https://docs.rs/alphabet/struct.Alphabet.html)and constants for alphabets commonly used in the wild.
- [display](https://docs.rs/display/index.html)
- Enables base64’d output anywhere you might use a `Display`implementation, like a format string.
- [engine](https://docs.rs/engine/index.html)
- Provides the [Engine](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html)abstraction and out of the box implementations.
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- Preconfigured engines for common use cases.
- [read](https://docs.rs/read/index.html)
- Implementations of `io::Read`to transparently decode base64.
- [write](https://docs.rs/write/index.html)
- Implementations of `io::Write`to transparently handle base64.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Decode](https://docs.rs/enum.DecodeError.html)- Error
- Errors that can occur while decoding.
- [Decode](https://docs.rs/enum.DecodeSliceError.html)- Slice - Error
- Errors that can occur while decoding into a slice.
- [Encode](https://docs.rs/enum.EncodeSliceError.html)- Slice - Error
- Errors that can occur while encoding into a slice.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [decode](https://docs.rs/fn.decode.html)- Deprecated
- Decode base64 using the `STANDARD`engine
- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_engine.html)- engine - Deprecated
- Decode from string reference as octets using the specified [Engine](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html).
- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_engine_slice.html)- engine_ - slice - Deprecated
- Decode the input into the provided output slice.
- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_engine_vec.html)- engine_ - vec - Deprecated
- Decode from string reference as octets.
- [decoded_](https://docs.rs/fn.decoded_len_estimate.html)- len_ - estimate
- Returns a conservative estimate of the decoded size of `encoded_len`base64 symbols (rounded up to the next group of 3 decoded bytes).
- [encode](https://docs.rs/fn.encode.html)- Deprecated
- Encode arbitrary octets as base64 using the `STANDARD`engine
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_engine.html)- engine - Deprecated
- Encode arbitrary octets as base64 using the provided `Engine`into a new`String`.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_engine_slice.html)- engine_ - slice - Deprecated
- Encode arbitrary octets as base64 into a supplied slice.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_engine_string.html)- engine_ - string - Deprecated
- Encode arbitrary octets as base64 into a supplied `String`.
- [encoded_](https://docs.rs/fn.encoded_len.html)- len
- Calculate the base64 encoded length for a given input length, optionally including any appropriate padding bytes.

[§](https://docs.rs#memory-allocation)Memory allocation

The [decode](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html#method.decode) and [encode](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html#method.encode) engine methods
allocate memory for their results – `decode` returns a `Vec<u8>` and
`encode` returns a `String`. To instead decode or encode into a buffer that
you allocated, use one of the alternative methods:

[§](https://docs.rs#decoding)Decoding

| Method | Output | Allocates memory |
|---|---|---|
| `Engine::decode` | returns a new `Vec<u8>` | always |
| `Engine::decode_vec` | appends to provided `Vec<u8>` | if `Vec`lacks capacity |
| `Engine::decode_slice` | writes to provided `&[u8]` | never |

[§](https://docs.rs#encoding)Encoding

| Method | Output | Allocates memory |
|---|---|---|
| `Engine::encode` | returns a new `String` | always |
| `Engine::encode_string` | appends to provided `String` | if `String`lacks capacity |
| `Engine::encode_slice` | writes to provided `&[u8]` | never |

[§](https://docs.rs#input-and-output)Input and output

The `base64` crate can [decode](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html#method.decode) and
[encode](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html#method.encode) values in memory, or
[ DecoderReader](https://docs.rs/read/struct.DecoderReader.html) and

[provide streaming decoding and encoding for any](https://docs.rs/write/struct.EncoderWriter.html)

`EncoderWriter`[readable](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Read.html)or

[writable](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Write.html)byte stream.

[§](https://docs.rs#decoding-1)Decoding

```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::STANDARD, read::DecoderReader};
let mut input = io::stdin();
let mut decoder = DecoderReader::new(&mut input, &STANDARD);
io::copy(&mut decoder, &mut io::stdout())?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#encoding-1)Encoding

```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::STANDARD, write::EncoderWriter};
let mut output = io::stdout();
let mut encoder = EncoderWriter::new(&mut output, &STANDARD);
io::copy(&mut io::stdin(), &mut encoder)?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#display)Display

If you only need a base64 representation for implementing the
[ Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html) trait, use

[:](https://docs.rs/display/struct.Base64Display.html)

`Base64Display````
use base64::{display::Base64Display, engine::general_purpose::STANDARD};
let value = Base64Display::new(b"\0\x01\x02\x03", &STANDARD);
assert_eq!("base64: AAECAw==", format!("base64: {}", value));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

If length calculations result in overflowing `usize`, a panic will result.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use engine::`- [Engine](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [alphabet](https://docs.rs/alphabet/index.html)
- Provides [Alphabet](https://docs.rs/alphabet/struct.Alphabet.html)and constants for alphabets commonly used in the wild.
- [display](https://docs.rs/display/index.html)
- Enables base64’d output anywhere you might use a `Display`implementation, like a format string.
- [engine](https://docs.rs/engine/index.html)
- Provides the [Engine](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html)abstraction and out of the box implementations.
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- Preconfigured engines for common use cases.
- [read](https://docs.rs/read/index.html)
- Implementations of `io::Read`to transparently decode base64.
- [write](https://docs.rs/write/index.html)
- Implementations of `io::Write`to transparently handle base64.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Decode](https://docs.rs/enum.DecodeError.html)- Error
- Errors that can occur while decoding.
- [Decode](https://docs.rs/enum.DecodeSliceError.html)- Slice - Error
- Errors that can occur while decoding into a slice.
- [Encode](https://docs.rs/enum.EncodeSliceError.html)- Slice - Error
- Errors that can occur while encoding into a slice.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [decode](https://docs.rs/fn.decode.html)- Deprecated
- Decode base64 using the `STANDARD`engine
- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_engine.html)- engine - Deprecated
- Decode from string reference as octets using the specified [Engine](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html).
- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_engine_slice.html)- engine_ - slice - Deprecated
- Decode the input into the provided output slice.
- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_engine_vec.html)- engine_ - vec - Deprecated
- Decode from string reference as octets.
- [decoded_](https://docs.rs/fn.decoded_len_estimate.html)- len_ - estimate
- Returns a conservative estimate of the decoded size of `encoded_len`base64 symbols (rounded up to the next group of 3 decoded bytes).
- [encode](https://docs.rs/fn.encode.html)- Deprecated
- Encode arbitrary octets as base64 using the `STANDARD`engine
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_engine.html)- engine - Deprecated
- Encode arbitrary octets as base64 using the provided `Engine`into a new`String`.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_engine_slice.html)- engine_ - slice - Deprecated
- Encode arbitrary octets as base64 into a supplied slice.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_engine_string.html)- engine_ - string - Deprecated
- Encode arbitrary octets as base64 into a supplied `String`.
- [encoded_](https://docs.rs/fn.encoded_len.html)- len
- Calculate the base64 encoded length for a given input length, optionally including any appropriate padding bytes.

# lib.rs - source

# base64/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! Correct, fast, and configurable [base64][] decoding and encoding. Base64
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//! transports binary data efficiently in contexts where only plain text is
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! allowed.
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//!
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! [base64]: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/Base64
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//!
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! # Usage
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//!
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! Use an [`Engine`] to decode or encode base64, configured with the base64
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! alphabet and padding behavior best suited to your application.
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//!
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! ## Engine setup
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//!
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! There is more than one way to encode a stream of bytes as “base64”.
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! Different applications use different encoding
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! [alphabets][alphabet::Alphabet] and
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! [padding behaviors][engine::general_purpose::GeneralPurposeConfig].
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//!
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! ### Encoding alphabet
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! Almost all base64 [alphabets][alphabet::Alphabet] use `A-Z`, `a-z`, and
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! `0-9`, which gives nearly 64 characters (26 + 26 + 10 = 62), but they differ
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! in their choice of their final 2.
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//!
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! Most applications use the [standard][alphabet::STANDARD] alphabet specified
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! in [RFC 4648][rfc-alphabet].  If that’s all you need, you can get started
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! quickly by using the pre-configured
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! [`STANDARD`][engine::general_purpose::STANDARD] engine, which is also available
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! in the [`prelude`] module as shown here, if you prefer a minimal `use`
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! footprint.
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!
[32](https://docs.rs#32)#![cfg_attr(feature = "alloc", doc = "```")]
[33](https://docs.rs#33)#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "alloc"), doc = "```ignore")]
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! use base64::prelude::*;
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//!
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! # fn main() -> Result<(), base64::DecodeError> {
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! assert_eq!(BASE64_STANDARD.decode(b"+uwgVQA=")?, b"\xFA\xEC\x20\x55\0");
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! assert_eq!(BASE64_STANDARD.encode(b"\xFF\xEC\x20\x55\0"), "/+wgVQA=");
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! # Ok(())
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! # }
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! ```
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//!
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! [rfc-alphabet]: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4648#section-4
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//!
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! Other common alphabets are available in the [`alphabet`] module.
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//!
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! #### URL-safe alphabet
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//!
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! The standard alphabet uses `+` and `/` as its two non-alphanumeric tokens,
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//! which cannot be safely used in URL’s without encoding them as `%2B` and
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! `%2F`.
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//!
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! To avoid that, some applications use a [“URL-safe” alphabet][alphabet::URL_SAFE],
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//! which uses `-` and `_` instead. To use that alternative alphabet, use the
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! [`URL_SAFE`][engine::general_purpose::URL_SAFE] engine. This example doesn't
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//! use [`prelude`] to show what a more explicit `use` would look like.
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//!
[58](https://docs.rs#58)#![cfg_attr(feature = "alloc", doc = "```")]
[59](https://docs.rs#59)#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "alloc"), doc = "```ignore")]
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! use base64::{engine::general_purpose::URL_SAFE, Engine as _};
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//!
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! # fn main() -> Result<(), base64::DecodeError> {
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! assert_eq!(URL_SAFE.decode(b"-uwgVQA=")?, b"\xFA\xEC\x20\x55\0");
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! assert_eq!(URL_SAFE.encode(b"\xFF\xEC\x20\x55\0"), "_-wgVQA=");
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//! # Ok(())
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! # }
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//! ```
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//!
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//! ### Padding characters
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//!
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//! Each base64 character represents 6 bits (2⁶ = 64) of the original binary
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! data, and every 3 bytes of input binary data will encode to 4 base64
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//! characters (8 bits × 3 = 6 bits × 4 = 24 bits).
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//!
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! When the input is not an even multiple of 3 bytes in length, [canonical][]
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//! base64 encoders insert padding characters at the end, so that the output
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//! length is always a multiple of 4:
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//!
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//! [canonical]: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4648#section-3.5
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//!
[81](https://docs.rs#81)#![cfg_attr(feature = "alloc", doc = "```")]
[82](https://docs.rs#82)#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "alloc"), doc = "```ignore")]
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//! use base64::{engine::general_purpose::STANDARD, Engine as _};
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//!
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//! assert_eq!(STANDARD.encode(b""),    "");
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//! assert_eq!(STANDARD.encode(b"f"),   "Zg==");
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//! assert_eq!(STANDARD.encode(b"fo"),  "Zm8=");
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//! assert_eq!(STANDARD.encode(b"foo"), "Zm9v");
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! ```
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//!
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//! Canonical encoding ensures that base64 encodings will be exactly the same,
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//! byte-for-byte, regardless of input length. But the `=` padding characters
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! aren’t necessary for decoding, and they may be omitted by using a
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//! [`NO_PAD`][engine::general_purpose::NO_PAD] configuration:
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//!
[96](https://docs.rs#96)#![cfg_attr(feature = "alloc", doc = "```")]
[97](https://docs.rs#97)#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "alloc"), doc = "```ignore")]
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//! use base64::{engine::general_purpose::STANDARD_NO_PAD, Engine as _};
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//!
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//! assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.encode(b""),    "");
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//! assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.encode(b"f"),   "Zg");
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//! assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.encode(b"fo"),  "Zm8");
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//! assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.encode(b"foo"), "Zm9v");
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//! ```
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//!
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//! The pre-configured `NO_PAD` engines will reject inputs containing padding
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//! `=` characters. To encode without padding and still accept padding while
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//! decoding, create an [engine][engine::general_purpose::GeneralPurpose] with
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//! that [padding mode][engine::DecodePaddingMode].
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//!
[111](https://docs.rs#111)#![cfg_attr(feature = "alloc", doc = "```")]
[112](https://docs.rs#112)#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "alloc"), doc = "```ignore")]
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//! # use base64::{engine::general_purpose::STANDARD_NO_PAD, Engine as _};
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//! assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.decode(b"Zm8="), Err(base64::DecodeError::InvalidPadding));
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//! ```
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//!
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//! ### Further customization
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//!
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//! Decoding and encoding behavior can be customized by creating an
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//! [engine][engine::GeneralPurpose] with an [alphabet][alphabet::Alphabet] and
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//! [padding configuration][engine::GeneralPurposeConfig]:
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//!
[123](https://docs.rs#123)#![cfg_attr(feature = "alloc", doc = "```")]
[124](https://docs.rs#124)#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "alloc"), doc = "```ignore")]
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//! use base64::{engine, alphabet, Engine as _};
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//!
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//! // bizarro-world base64: +/ as the first symbols instead of the last
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//! let alphabet =
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//!     alphabet::Alphabet::new("+/ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789")
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//!     .unwrap();
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//!
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//! // a very weird config that encodes with padding but requires no padding when decoding...?
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//! let crazy_config = engine::GeneralPurposeConfig::new()
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//!     .with_decode_allow_trailing_bits(true)
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//!     .with_encode_padding(true)
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//!     .with_decode_padding_mode(engine::DecodePaddingMode::RequireNone);
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//!
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//! let crazy_engine = engine::GeneralPurpose::new(&alphabet, crazy_config);
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//!
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//! let encoded = crazy_engine.encode(b"abc 123");
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//!
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//! ```
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//!
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//! ## Memory allocation
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//!
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//! The [decode][Engine::decode()] and [encode][Engine::encode()] engine methods
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//! allocate memory for their results – `decode` returns a `Vec<u8>` and
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//! `encode` returns a `String`. To instead decode or encode into a buffer that
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//! you allocated, use one of the alternative methods:
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//!
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//! #### Decoding
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//!
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//! | Method                     | Output                        | Allocates memory              |
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//! | -------------------------- | ----------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//! | [`Engine::decode`]         | returns a new `Vec<u8>`       | always                        |
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//! | [`Engine::decode_vec`]     | appends to provided `Vec<u8>` | if `Vec` lacks capacity       |
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//! | [`Engine::decode_slice`]   | writes to provided `&[u8]`    | never
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//!
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//! #### Encoding
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//!
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//! | Method                     | Output                       | Allocates memory               |
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//! | -------------------------- | ---------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//! | [`Engine::encode`]         | returns a new `String`       | always                         |
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//! | [`Engine::encode_string`]  | appends to provided `String` | if `String` lacks capacity     |
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//! | [`Engine::encode_slice`]   | writes to provided `&[u8]`   | never                          |
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//!
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//! ## Input and output
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//!
[169](https://docs.rs#169)//! The `base64` crate can [decode][Engine::decode()] and
[170](https://docs.rs#170)//! [encode][Engine::encode()] values in memory, or
[171](https://docs.rs#171)//! [`DecoderReader`][read::DecoderReader] and
[172](https://docs.rs#172)//! [`EncoderWriter`][write::EncoderWriter] provide streaming decoding and
[173](https://docs.rs#173)//! encoding for any [readable][std::io::Read] or [writable][std::io::Write]
[174](https://docs.rs#174)//! byte stream.
[175](https://docs.rs#175)//!
[176](https://docs.rs#176)//! #### Decoding
[177](https://docs.rs#177)//!
[178](https://docs.rs#178)#![cfg_attr(feature = "std", doc = "```")]
[179](https://docs.rs#179)#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "std"), doc = "```ignore")]
[180](https://docs.rs#180)//! # use std::io;
[181](https://docs.rs#181)//! use base64::{engine::general_purpose::STANDARD, read::DecoderReader};
[182](https://docs.rs#182)//!
[183](https://docs.rs#183)//! # fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
[184](https://docs.rs#184)//! let mut input = io::stdin();
[185](https://docs.rs#185)//! let mut decoder = DecoderReader::new(&mut input, &STANDARD);
[186](https://docs.rs#186)//! io::copy(&mut decoder, &mut io::stdout())?;
[187](https://docs.rs#187)//! # Ok(())
[188](https://docs.rs#188)//! # }
[189](https://docs.rs#189)//! ```
[190](https://docs.rs#190)//!
[191](https://docs.rs#191)//! #### Encoding
[192](https://docs.rs#192)//!
[193](https://docs.rs#193)#![cfg_attr(feature = "std", doc = "```")]
[194](https://docs.rs#194)#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "std"), doc = "```ignore")]
[195](https://docs.rs#195)//! # use std::io;
[196](https://docs.rs#196)//! use base64::{engine::general_purpose::STANDARD, write::EncoderWriter};
[197](https://docs.rs#197)//!
[198](https://docs.rs#198)//! # fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
[199](https://docs.rs#199)//! let mut output = io::stdout();
[200](https://docs.rs#200)//! let mut encoder = EncoderWriter::new(&mut output, &STANDARD);
[201](https://docs.rs#201)//! io::copy(&mut io::stdin(), &mut encoder)?;
[202](https://docs.rs#202)//! # Ok(())
[203](https://docs.rs#203)//! # }
[204](https://docs.rs#204)//! ```
[205](https://docs.rs#205)//!
[206](https://docs.rs#206)//! #### Display
[207](https://docs.rs#207)//!
[208](https://docs.rs#208)//! If you only need a base64 representation for implementing the
[209](https://docs.rs#209)//! [`Display`][std::fmt::Display] trait, use
[210](https://docs.rs#210)//! [`Base64Display`][display::Base64Display]:
[211](https://docs.rs#211)//!
[212](https://docs.rs#212)//! ```
[213](https://docs.rs#213)//! use base64::{display::Base64Display, engine::general_purpose::STANDARD};
[214](https://docs.rs#214)//!
[215](https://docs.rs#215)//! let value = Base64Display::new(b"\0\x01\x02\x03", &STANDARD);
[216](https://docs.rs#216)//! assert_eq!("base64: AAECAw==", format!("base64: {}", value));
[217](https://docs.rs#217)//! ```
[218](https://docs.rs#218)//!
[219](https://docs.rs#219)//! # Panics
[220](https://docs.rs#220)//!
[221](https://docs.rs#221)//! If length calculations result in overflowing `usize`, a panic will result.
[222](https://docs.rs#222)
[223](https://docs.rs#223)#![cfg_attr(feature = "cargo-clippy", allow(clippy::cast_lossless))]
[224](https://docs.rs#224)#![deny(
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    missing_docs,
[226](https://docs.rs#226)    trivial_casts,

    ) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), [DecodeError](https://docs.rs/enum.DecodeError.html)> { ... }
}## Expand description

An `Engine` provides low-level encoding and decoding operations that all other higher-level parts of the API use. Users of the library will generally not need to implement this.

Different implementations offer different characteristics. The library currently ships with
[GeneralPurpose](https://docs.rs/general_purpose/struct.GeneralPurpose.html) that offers good speed and works on any CPU, with more choices
coming later, like a constant-time one when side channel resistance is called for, and vendor-specific vectorized ones for more speed.

See [general_purpose::STANDARD_NO_PAD](https://docs.rs/general_purpose/constant.STANDARD_NO_PAD.html) if you just want standard base64. Otherwise, when possible, it’s
recommended to store the engine in a `const` so that references to it won’t pose any lifetime
issues, and to avoid repeating the cost of engine setup.

Since almost nobody will need to implement `Engine`, docs for internal methods are hidden.

## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

Encode arbitrary octets as base64 using the provided `Engine`.
Returns a `String`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use base64::{Engine as _, engine::{self, general_purpose}, alphabet};
let b64 = general_purpose::STANDARD.encode(b"hello world~");
println!("{}", b64);
const CUSTOM_ENGINE: engine::GeneralPurpose =
    engine::GeneralPurpose::new(&alphabet::URL_SAFE, general_purpose::NO_PAD);
let b64_url = CUSTOM_ENGINE.encode(b"hello internet~");
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/base64/engine/mod.rs.html#155-168)

#### fn [encode_string](https://docs.rs#method.encode_string)<T: [AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]>>(&self, input: T, output_buf: &mut [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html))

Encode arbitrary octets as base64 into a supplied `String`.
Writes into the supplied `String`, which may allocate if its internal buffer isn’t big enough.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

```
use base64::{Engine as _, engine::{self, general_purpose}, alphabet};
const CUSTOM_ENGINE: engine::GeneralPurpose =
    engine::GeneralPurpose::new(&alphabet::URL_SAFE, general_purpose::NO_PAD);
fn main() {
    let mut buf = String::new();
    general_purpose::STANDARD.encode_string(b"hello world~", &mut buf);
    println!("{}", buf);
    buf.clear();
    CUSTOM_ENGINE.encode_string(b"hello internet~", &mut buf);
    println!("{}", buf);
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/base64/engine/mod.rs.html#194-222)#### fn [encode_slice](https://docs.rs#method.encode_slice)<T: [AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]>>(

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/base64/engine/mod.rs.html#194-222)

#### fn [encode_slice](https://docs.rs#method.encode_slice)<T: [AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]>>(
    &self,
    input: T,
    output_buf: &mut [[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)],
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), [EncodeSliceError](https://docs.rs/enum.EncodeSliceError.html)>

Encode arbitrary octets as base64 into a supplied slice. Writes into the supplied output buffer.

This is useful if you wish to avoid allocation entirely (e.g. encoding into a stack-resident or statically-allocated buffer).

[§](https://docs.rs#example-2)Example

```
use base64::{Engine as _, engine::general_purpose};
let s = b"hello internet!";
let mut buf = Vec::new();
// make sure we'll have a slice big enough for base64 + padding
buf.resize(s.len() * 4 / 3 + 4, 0);
let bytes_written = general_purpose::STANDARD.encode_slice(s, &mut buf).unwrap();
// shorten our vec down to just what was written
buf.truncate(bytes_written);
assert_eq!(s, general_purpose::STANDARD.decode(&buf).unwrap().as_slice());
```
Decode the input into a new `Vec`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-3)Example

```
use base64::{Engine as _, alphabet, engine::{self, general_purpose}};
let bytes = general_purpose::STANDARD
    .decode("aGVsbG8gd29ybGR+Cg==").unwrap();
println!("{:?}", bytes);
// custom engine setup
let bytes_url = engine::GeneralPurpose::new(
             &alphabet::URL_SAFE,
             general_purpose::NO_PAD)
    .decode("aGVsbG8gaW50ZXJuZXR-Cg").unwrap();
println!("{:?}", bytes_url);
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/base64/engine/mod.rs.html#302-339)

#### fn [decode_vec](https://docs.rs#method.decode_vec)<T: [AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]>>(
    &self,
    input: T,
    buffer: &mut [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)>,
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [DecodeError](https://docs.rs/enum.DecodeError.html)>

Decode the `input` into the supplied `buffer`.

Writes into the supplied `Vec`, which may allocate if its internal buffer isn’t big enough.
Returns a `Result` containing an empty tuple, aka `()`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-4)Example

```
use base64::{Engine as _, alphabet, engine::{self, general_purpose}};
const CUSTOM_ENGINE: engine::GeneralPurpose =
    engine::GeneralPurpose::new(&alphabet::URL_SAFE, general_purpose::PAD);
fn main() {
    use base64::Engine;
    let mut buffer = Vec::<u8>::new();
    // with the default engine
    general_purpose::STANDARD
        .decode_vec("aGVsbG8gd29ybGR+Cg==", &mut buffer,).unwrap();
    println!("{:?}", buffer);
    buffer.clear();
    // with a custom engine
    CUSTOM_ENGINE.decode_vec(
        "aGVsbG8gaW50ZXJuZXR-Cg==",
        &mut buffer,
    ).unwrap();
    println!("{:?}", buffer);
}
```

#### fn [decode_slice](https://docs.rs#method.decode_slice)<T: [AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]>>(
    &self,
    input: T,
    output: &mut [[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)],
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), [DecodeSliceError](https://docs.rs/enum.DecodeSliceError.html)>

Decode the input into the provided output slice.

Returns the number of bytes written to the slice, or an error if `output` is smaller than
the estimated decoded length.

This will not write any bytes past exactly what is decoded (no stray garbage bytes at the end).

See [crate::decoded_len_estimate](https://docs.rs/fn.decoded_len_estimate.html) for calculating buffer sizes.

See [Engine::decode_slice_unchecked](https://docs.rs/trait.Engine.html#method.decode_slice_unchecked) for a version that panics instead of returning an error
if the output buffer is too small.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/base64/engine/mod.rs.html#393-418)#### fn [decode_slice_unchecked](https://docs.rs#method.decode_slice_unchecked)<T: [AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]>>(
    &self,
    input: T,
    output: &mut [[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)],
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), [DecodeError](https://docs.rs/enum.DecodeError.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/base64/engine/mod.rs.html#393-418)

#### fn [decode_slice_unchecked](https://docs.rs#method.decode_slice_unchecked)<T: [AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]>>(
    &self,
    input: T,
    output: &mut [[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)],

Decode the input into the provided output slice.

Returns the number of bytes written to the slice.

This will not write any bytes past exactly what is decoded (no stray garbage bytes at the end).

See [crate::decoded_len_estimate](https://docs.rs/fn.decoded_len_estimate.html) for calculating buffer sizes.

See [Engine::decode_slice](https://docs.rs/trait.Engine.html#method.decode_slice) for a version that returns an error instead of panicking if the output
buffer is too small.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if the provided output buffer is too small for the decoded data.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# GeneralPurpose in base64::engine::general_purpose - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/base64/0.22.1/base64/engine/general_purpose/struct.GeneralPurpose.html

`pub struct GeneralPurpose { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A general-purpose base64 engine.

- It uses no vector CPU instructions, so it will work on any system.
- It is reasonably fast (~2-3GiB/s).
- It is not constant-time, though, so it is vulnerable to timing side-channel attacks. For loading cryptographic keys, etc, it is suggested to use the forthcoming constant-time implementation.

# DecodePaddingMode in base64::engine - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/base64/0.22.1/base64/engine/enum.DecodePaddingMode.html

```
pub enum DecodePaddingMode {
    Indifferent,
    RequireCanonical,
    RequireNone,
}
```
## Expand description

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Indifferent)

### Indifferent

Canonical padding is allowed, but any fewer padding bytes than that is also allowed.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.RequireCanonical)

### RequireCanonical

Padding must be canonical (0, 1, or 2 `=` as needed to produce a 4 byte suffix).

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.RequireNone)

### RequireNone

Padding must be absent – for when you want predictable padding, without any wasted bytes.

# DecoderReader in base64::read - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/base64/0.22.1/base64/read/struct.DecoderReader.html

## Expand description

A `Read` implementation that decodes base64 data read from an underlying reader.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use std::io::Read;
use std::io::Cursor;
use base64::engine::general_purpose;
// use a cursor as the simplest possible `Read` -- in real code this is probably a file, etc.
let mut wrapped_reader = Cursor::new(b"YXNkZg==");
let mut decoder = base64::read::DecoderReader::new(
    &mut wrapped_reader,
    &general_purpose::STANDARD);
// handle errors as you normally would
let mut result = Vec::new();
decoder.read_to_end(&mut result).unwrap();
assert_eq!(b"asdf", &result[..]);
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/base64/read/decoder.rs.html#214-216)#### pub fn [into_inner](https://docs.rs#method.into_inner)(self) -> R

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/base64/read/decoder.rs.html#214-216)

#### pub fn [into_inner](https://docs.rs#method.into_inner)(self) -> R

Unwraps this `DecoderReader`, returning the base reader which it reads base64 encoded
input from.

Because `DecoderReader` performs internal buffering, the state of the inner reader is
unspecified. This function is mainly provided because the inner reader type may provide
additional functionality beyond the `Read` implementation which may still be useful.

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

Decode input from the wrapped reader.

Under non-error circumstances, this returns `Ok` with the value being the number of bytes
written in `buf`.

Where possible, this function buffers base64 to minimize the number of read() calls to the delegate reader.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

Any errors emitted by the delegate reader are returned. Decoding errors due to invalid
base64 are also possible, and will have `io::ErrorKind::InvalidData`.

# EncoderWriter in base64::write - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/base64/0.22.1/base64/write/struct.EncoderWriter.html

## Expand description

A `Write` implementation that base64 encodes data before delegating to the wrapped writer.

Because base64 has special handling for the end of the input data (padding, etc), there’s a
`finish()` method on this type that encodes any leftover input bytes and adds padding if
appropriate. It’s called automatically when deallocated (see the `Drop` implementation), but
any error that occurs when invoking the underlying writer will be suppressed. If you want to
handle such errors, call `finish()` yourself.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use std::io::Write;
use base64::engine::general_purpose;
// use a vec as the simplest possible `Write` -- in real code this is probably a file, etc.
let mut enc = base64::write::EncoderWriter::new(Vec::new(), &general_purpose::STANDARD);
// handle errors as you normally would
enc.write_all(b"asdf").unwrap();
// could leave this out to be called by Drop, if you don't care
// about handling errors or getting the delegate writer back
let delegate = enc.finish().unwrap();
// base64 was written to the writer
assert_eq!(b"YXNkZg==", &delegate[..]);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Calling `write()` (or related methods) or `finish()` after `finish()` has completed without
error is invalid and will panic.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

Base64 encoding itself does not generate errors, but errors from the wrapped writer will be
returned as per the contract of `Write`.

[§](https://docs.rs#performance)Performance

It has some minor performance loss compared to encoding slices (a couple percent). It does not do any heap allocation.

[§](https://docs.rs#limitations)Limitations

Owing to the specification of the `write` and `flush` methods on the `Write` trait and their
implications for a buffering implementation, these methods may not behave as expected. In
particular, calling `write_all` on this interface may fail with `io::ErrorKind::WriteZero`.
See the documentation of the `Write` trait implementation for further details.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/base64/write/encoder.rs.html#96-246)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-EncoderWriter%3C'e,+E,+W%3E)### impl<'e, E: [Engine](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html), W: [Write](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Write.html)> [EncoderWriter](https://docs.rs/struct.EncoderWriter.html)<'e, E, W>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/base64/write/encoder.rs.html#96-246)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-EncoderWriter%3C'e,+E,+W%3E)

### impl<'e, E: [Engine](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html), W: [Write](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Write.html)> [EncoderWriter](https://docs.rs/struct.EncoderWriter.html)<'e, E, W>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/base64/write/encoder.rs.html#98-108)#### pub fn [new](https://docs.rs#method.new)(delegate: W, engine: [&'e E](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)) -> [EncoderWriter](https://docs.rs/struct.EncoderWriter.html)<'e, E, W> [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/base64/write/encoder.rs.html#98-108)

#### pub fn [new](https://docs.rs#method.new)(delegate: W, engine: [&'e E](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)) -> [EncoderWriter](https://docs.rs/struct.EncoderWriter.html)<'e, E, W> [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

Create a new encoder that will write to the provided delegate writer.

Encode all remaining buffered data and write it, including any trailing incomplete input triples and associated padding.

Once this succeeds, no further writes or calls to this method are allowed.

This may write to the delegate writer multiple times if the delegate writer does not accept
all input provided to its `write` each invocation.

If you don’t care about error handling, it is not necessary to call this function, as the equivalent finalization is done by the Drop impl.

Returns the writer that this was constructed around.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-1)Errors

The first error that is not of `ErrorKind::Interrupted` will be returned.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/base64/write/encoder.rs.html#241-245)#### pub fn [into_inner](https://docs.rs#method.into_inner)(self) -> W

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/base64/write/encoder.rs.html#241-245)

#### pub fn [into_inner](https://docs.rs#method.into_inner)(self) -> W

Unwraps this `EncoderWriter`, returning the base writer it writes base64 encoded output
to.

Normally this method should not be needed, since `finish()` returns the inner writer if
it completes successfully. That will also ensure all data has been flushed, which the
`into_inner()` function does *not* do.

Calling this method after `finish()` has completed successfully will panic, since the
writer has already been returned.

This method may be useful if the writer implements additional APIs beyond the `Write`
trait. Note that the inner writer might be in an error state or have an incomplete
base64 string written to it.

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

Encode input and then write to the delegate writer.

Under non-error circumstances, this returns `Ok` with the value being the number of bytes
of `input` consumed. The value may be `0`, which interacts poorly with `write_all`, which
interprets `Ok(0)` as an error, despite it being allowed by the contract of `write`. See
[https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/56889](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/56889) for more on that.

If the previous call to `write` provided more (encoded) data than the delegate writer could
accept in a single call to its `write`, the remaining data is buffered. As long as buffered
data is present, subsequent calls to `write` will try to write the remaining buffered data
to the delegate and return either `Ok(0)` – and therefore not consume any of `input` – or
an error.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-2)Errors

Any errors emitted by the delegate writer are returned.

Because this is usually treated as OK to call multiple times, it will *not* flush any
incomplete chunks of input or write padding.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-3)Errors

The first error that is not of [ ErrorKind::Interrupted](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/io/error/enum.ErrorKind.html#variant.Interrupted) will be returned.

`write_all_vectored`)## Auto Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#synthetic-implementations)

# Base64Display in base64::display - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/base64/0.22.1/base64/display/struct.Base64Display.html

# base64::write - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/base64/0.22.1/base64/write/index.html

## Expand description

Implementations of `io::Write` to transparently handle base64.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Encoder](https://docs.rs/struct.EncoderStringWriter.html)- String - Writer
- A `Write`implementation that base64-encodes data using the provided config and accumulates the resulting base64 utf8`&str`in a[StrConsumer](https://docs.rs/trait.StrConsumer.html)implementation (typically`String`), which is then exposed via`into_inner()`.
- [Encoder](https://docs.rs/struct.EncoderWriter.html)- Writer
- A `Write`implementation that base64 encodes data before delegating to the wrapped writer.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [StrConsumer](https://docs.rs/trait.StrConsumer.html)
- An abstraction around consuming `str`s produced by base64 encoding.

---

# DecodeError in base64 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/base64/0.22.1/base64/enum.DecodeError.html

```
pub enum DecodeError {
    InvalidByte(
```
[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), [u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)),
    InvalidLength([usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)),
    InvalidLastSymbol([usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), [u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)),
    InvalidPadding,
}## Expand description

Errors that can occur while decoding.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.InvalidByte)

An invalid byte was found in the input. The offset and offending byte are provided.

Padding characters (`=`) interspersed in the encoded form are invalid, as they may only
be present as the last 0-2 bytes of input.

This error may also indicate that extraneous trailing input bytes are present, causing otherwise valid padding to no longer be the last bytes of input.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.InvalidLength)

### InvalidLength([usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html))

The length of the input, as measured in valid base64 symbols, is invalid. There must be 2-4 symbols in the last input quad.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.InvalidLastSymbol)

The last non-padding input symbol’s encoded 6 bits have nonzero bits that will be discarded.
This is indicative of corrupted or truncated Base64.
Unlike [DecodeError::InvalidByte](https://docs.rs/enum.DecodeError.html#variant.InvalidByte), which reports symbols that aren’t in the alphabet,
this error is for symbols that are in the alphabet but represent nonsensical encodings.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.InvalidPadding)

### InvalidPadding

The nature of the padding was not as configured: absent or incorrect when it must be canonical, or present when it must be absent, etc.

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/base64/decode.rs.html#9)

# encoded_len in base64 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/base64/0.22.1/base64/fn.encoded_len.html

## Expand description

Calculate the base64 encoded length for a given input length, optionally including any appropriate padding bytes.

Returns `None` if the encoded length can’t be represented in `usize`. This will happen for
input lengths in approximately the top quarter of the range of `usize`.

---

# base64 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/base64/latest/base64/

## Expand description

Correct, fast, and configurable [base64](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/Base64) decoding and encoding. Base64
transports binary data efficiently in contexts where only plain text is
allowed.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Use an [ Engine](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html) to decode or encode base64, configured with the base64
alphabet and padding behavior best suited to your application.

[§](https://docs.rs#engine-setup)Engine setup

There is more than one way to encode a stream of bytes as “base64”.
Different applications use different encoding
[alphabets](https://docs.rs/alphabet/struct.Alphabet.html) and
[padding behaviors](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/struct.GeneralPurposeConfig.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#encoding-alphabet)Encoding alphabet

Almost all base64 [alphabets](https://docs.rs/alphabet/struct.Alphabet.html) use `A-Z`, `a-z`, and
`0-9`, which gives nearly 64 characters (26 + 26 + 10 = 62), but they differ
in their choice of their final 2.

Most applications use the [standard](https://docs.rs/alphabet/constant.STANDARD.html) alphabet specified
in [RFC 4648](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4648#section-4).  If that’s all you need, you can get started
quickly by using the pre-configured
[ STANDARD](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/constant.STANDARD.html) engine, which is also available
in the

[module as shown here, if you prefer a minimal](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)

`prelude``use`
footprint.```
use base64::prelude::*;
assert_eq!(BASE64_STANDARD.decode(b"+uwgVQA=")?, b"\xFA\xEC\x20\x55\0");
assert_eq!(BASE64_STANDARD.encode(b"\xFF\xEC\x20\x55\0"), "/+wgVQA=");
```
Other common alphabets are available in the [ alphabet](https://docs.rs/alphabet/index.html) module.

[§](https://docs.rs#url-safe-alphabet)URL-safe alphabet

The standard alphabet uses `+` and `/` as its two non-alphanumeric tokens,
which cannot be safely used in URL’s without encoding them as `%2B` and
`%2F`.

To avoid that, some applications use a [“URL-safe” alphabet](https://docs.rs/alphabet/constant.URL_SAFE.html),
which uses `-` and `_` instead. To use that alternative alphabet, use the
[ URL_SAFE](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/constant.URL_SAFE.html) engine. This example doesn’t
use

[to show what a more explicit](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)

`prelude``use` would look like.```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::URL_SAFE, Engine as _};
assert_eq!(URL_SAFE.decode(b"-uwgVQA=")?, b"\xFA\xEC\x20\x55\0");
assert_eq!(URL_SAFE.encode(b"\xFF\xEC\x20\x55\0"), "_-wgVQA=");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#padding-characters)Padding characters

Each base64 character represents 6 bits (2⁶ = 64) of the original binary data, and every 3 bytes of input binary data will encode to 4 base64 characters (8 bits × 3 = 6 bits × 4 = 24 bits).

When the input is not an even multiple of 3 bytes in length, [canonical](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4648#section-3.5)
base64 encoders insert padding characters at the end, so that the output
length is always a multiple of 4:

```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::STANDARD, Engine as _};
assert_eq!(STANDARD.encode(b""),    "");
assert_eq!(STANDARD.encode(b"f"),   "Zg==");
assert_eq!(STANDARD.encode(b"fo"),  "Zm8=");
assert_eq!(STANDARD.encode(b"foo"), "Zm9v");
```
Canonical encoding ensures that base64 encodings will be exactly the same,
byte-for-byte, regardless of input length. But the `=` padding characters
aren’t necessary for decoding, and they may be omitted by using a
[ NO_PAD](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/constant.NO_PAD.html) configuration:

```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::STANDARD_NO_PAD, Engine as _};
assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.encode(b""),    "");
assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.encode(b"f"),   "Zg");
assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.encode(b"fo"),  "Zm8");
assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.encode(b"foo"), "Zm9v");
```
The pre-configured `NO_PAD` engines will reject inputs containing padding
`=` characters. To encode without padding and still accept padding while
decoding, create an [engine](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/struct.GeneralPurpose.html) with
that [padding mode](https://docs.rs/engine/enum.DecodePaddingMode.html).

`assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.decode(b"Zm8="), Err(base64::DecodeError::InvalidPadding));`[§](https://docs.rs#further-customization)Further customization

Decoding and encoding behavior can be customized by creating an
[engine](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/struct.GeneralPurpose.html) with an [alphabet](https://docs.rs/alphabet/struct.Alphabet.html) and
[padding configuration](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/struct.GeneralPurposeConfig.html):

```
use base64::{engine, alphabet, Engine as _};
// bizarro-world base64: +/ as the first symbols instead of the last
let alphabet =
    alphabet::Alphabet::new("+/ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789")
    .unwrap();
// a very weird config that encodes with padding but requires no padding when decoding...?
let crazy_config = engine::GeneralPurposeConfig::new()
    .with_decode_allow_trailing_bits(true)
    .with_encode_padding(true)
    .with_decode_padding_mode(engine::DecodePaddingMode::RequireNone);
let crazy_engine = engine::GeneralPurpose::new(&alphabet, crazy_config);
let encoded = crazy_engine.encode(b"abc 123");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#memory-allocation)Memory allocation

The [decode](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html#method.decode) and [encode](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html#method.encode) engine methods
allocate memory for their results – `decode` returns a `Vec<u8>` and
`encode` returns a `String`. To instead decode or encode into a buffer that
you allocated, use one of the alternative methods:

[§](https://docs.rs#decoding)Decoding

| Method | Output | Allocates memory |
|---|---|---|
| `Engine::decode` | returns a new `Vec<u8>` | always |
| `Engine::decode_vec` | appends to provided `Vec<u8>` | if `Vec`lacks capacity |
| `Engine::decode_slice` | writes to provided `&[u8]` | never |

[§](https://docs.rs#encoding)Encoding

| Method | Output | Allocates memory |
|---|---|---|
| `Engine::encode` | returns a new `String` | always |
| `Engine::encode_string` | appends to provided `String` | if `String`lacks capacity |
| `Engine::encode_slice` | writes to provided `&[u8]` | never |

[§](https://docs.rs#input-and-output)Input and output

The `base64` crate can [decode](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html#method.decode) and
[encode](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html#method.encode) values in memory, or
[ DecoderReader](https://docs.rs/read/struct.DecoderReader.html) and

[provide streaming decoding and encoding for any](https://docs.rs/write/struct.EncoderWriter.html)

`EncoderWriter`[readable](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Read.html)or

[writable](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Write.html)byte stream.

[§](https://docs.rs#decoding-1)Decoding

```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::STANDARD, read::DecoderReader};
let mut input = io::stdin();
let mut decoder = DecoderReader::new(&mut input, &STANDARD);
io::copy(&mut decoder, &mut io::stdout())?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#encoding-1)Encoding

```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::STANDARD, write::EncoderWriter};
let mut output = io::stdout();
let mut encoder = EncoderWriter::new(&mut output, &STANDARD);
io::copy(&mut io::stdin(), &mut encoder)?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#display)Display

If you only need a base64 representation for implementing the
[ Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html) trait, use

[:](https://docs.rs/display/struct.Base64Display.html)

`Base64Display````
use base64::{display::Base64Display, engine::general_purpose::STANDARD};
let value = Base64Display::new(b"\0\x01\x02\x03", &STANDARD);
assert_eq!("base64: AAECAw==", format!("base64: {}", value));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

If length calculations result in overflowing `usize`, a panic will result.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use engine::`- [Engine](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [alphabet](https://docs.rs/alphabet/index.html)
- Provides [Alphabet](https://docs.rs/alphabet/struct.Alphabet.html)and constants for alphabets commonly used in the wild.
- [display](https://docs.rs/display/index.html)
- Enables base64’d output anywhere you might use a `Display`implementation, like a format string.
- [engine](https://docs.rs/engine/index.html)
- Provides the [Engine](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html)abstraction and out of the box implementations.
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- Preconfigured engines for common use cases.
- [read](https://docs.rs/read/index.html)
- Implementations of `io::Read`to transparently decode base64.
- [write](https://docs.rs/write/index.html)
- Implementations of `io::Write`to transparently handle base64.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Decode](https://docs.rs/enum.DecodeError.html)- Error
- Errors that can occur while decoding.
- [Decode](https://docs.rs/enum.DecodeSliceError.html)- Slice - Error
- Errors that can occur while decoding into a slice.
- [Encode](https://docs.rs/enum.EncodeSliceError.html)- Slice - Error
- Errors that can occur while encoding into a slice.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [decode](https://docs.rs/fn.decode.html)- Deprecated
- Decode base64 using the `STANDARD`engine
- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_engine.html)- engine - Deprecated
- Decode from string reference as octets using the specified [Engine](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html).
- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_engine_slice.html)- engine_ - slice - Deprecated
- Decode the input into the provided output slice.
- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_engine_vec.html)- engine_ - vec - Deprecated
- Decode from string reference as octets.
- [decoded_](https://docs.rs/fn.decoded_len_estimate.html)- len_ - estimate
- Returns a conservative estimate of the decoded size of `encoded_len`base64 symbols (rounded up to the next group of 3 decoded bytes).
- [encode](https://docs.rs/fn.encode.html)- Deprecated
- Encode arbitrary octets as base64 using the `STANDARD`engine
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_engine.html)- engine - Deprecated
- Encode arbitrary octets as base64 using the provided `Engine`into a new`String`.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_engine_slice.html)- engine_ - slice - Deprecated
- Encode arbitrary octets as base64 into a supplied slice.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_engine_string.html)- engine_ - string - Deprecated
- Encode arbitrary octets as base64 into a supplied `String`.
- [encoded_](https://docs.rs/fn.encoded_len.html)- len
- Calculate the base64 encoded length for a given input length, optionally including any appropriate padding bytes.

# once_cell 1.21.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/once_cell/^1

# Overview

`once_cell` provides two new cell-like types, `unsync::OnceCell` and `sync::OnceCell`. `OnceCell`
might store arbitrary non-`Copy` types, can be assigned to at most once and provide direct access
to the stored contents. In a nutshell, API looks *roughly* like this:

```
```
Note that, like with `RefCell` and `Mutex`, the `set` method requires only a shared reference.
Because of the single assignment restriction `get` can return an `&T` instead of `Ref<T>`
or `MutexGuard<T>`.

`once_cell` also has a `Lazy<T>` type, build on top of `OnceCell` which provides the same API as
the `lazy_static!` macro, but without using any macros:

```
use ;
use Lazy;
static GLOBAL_DATA:  = new;
```
More patterns and use-cases are in the [docs](https://docs.rs/once_cell/)!

# Related crates

- [double-checked-cell](https://github.com/niklasf/double-checked-cell)
- [lazy-init](https://crates.io/crates/lazy-init)
- [lazycell](https://crates.io/crates/lazycell)
- [mitochondria](https://crates.io/crates/mitochondria)
- [lazy_static](https://crates.io/crates/lazy_static)
- [async_once_cell](https://crates.io/crates/async_once_cell)
- [generic_once_cell](https://crates.io/crates/generic_once_cell)(bring your own mutex)

Parts of `once_cell` API are included into `std` [as of Rust 1.70.0](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/105587).

# strum 0.25.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/strum/^0.25

# Strum

Strum is a set of macros and traits for working with enums and strings easier in Rust.

The full version of the README can be found on [GitHub](https://github.com/Peternator7/strum).

# Including Strum in Your Project

Import strum and `strum_macros` into your project by adding the following lines to your
Cargo.toml. `strum_macros` contains the macros needed to derive all the traits in Strum.

```
[]
 = "0.25"
 = "0.25"
# You can also access strum_macros exports directly through strum using the "derive" feature
 = {  = "0.25",  = ["derive"] }
```
